sections.normalized_html: Given that [MATH: x], [MATH: 3x], [MATH: 36] are the first three terms of a geometric sequence, find [MATH: x.]
sections.readable_text: Given that [MATH: x], [MATH: 3x], [MATH: 36] are the first three terms of a geometric sequence, find [MATH: x.]

sections.normalized_html:
The first three terms are as follows:

[MATH: a_{1} = x, a_{2} = 3x, a_{3} = 36.]

The common ratio of the first two terms is

[MATH: r = (a_{2})/(a_{1}) = (3x)/(x) = 3.]

On the other hand, the common ratio of the second and third terms is

[MATH: r = (a_{3})/(a_{2}) = (36)/(3x) = (12)/(x).]

So, by equating the values for [MATH: r] and solving for [MATH: x,] we conclude that [MATH: 3|= (12)/(x); 3x|= 12; x|= 4.]

items.title: Identifying Geometric Sequences

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the sequences below are geometric sequences?

  1. [MATH: 2, \: 4, \: 8, \: 16, \: \ldots]

  2. [MATH: 1, \: -\dfrac{1}{3}, \: \dfrac{1}{9}, \: -\dfrac{1}{27}, \: \ldots]

sections.readable_text:
Which of the sequences below are geometric sequences?

1. [MATH: 2, \: 4, \: 8, \: 16, \: \ldots]
2. [MATH: 1, \: -\dfrac{1}{3}, \: \dfrac{1}{9}, \: -\dfrac{1}{27}, \: \ldots]
3. [MATH: 4, \: 8, \: 12, \: 16, \: \ldots]

sections.normalized_html:
A sequence is geometric if there is a common ratio between its terms. Let's check each sequence in turn.

  • Sequence I is geometric. For each pair of consecutive terms, the common ratio is the same: [MATH: (a_{2})/(a_{1}) = (4)/(2)|= 2; (a_{3})/(a_{2}) = (8)/(4)|= 2; (a_{4})/(a_{3}) = (16)/(8)|= 2]

  • Sequence II is also geometric. Again, for each pair of consecutive terms, the common ratio is the same: [MATH: (a_{2})/(a_{1}) = ((− (1)/(3)))/(1)|= − (1)/(3); (a_{3})/(a_{2}) = (((1)/(9)))/((− (1)/(3)))|= − (1)/(3); (a_{4})/(a_{3}) = ((− (1)/(27)))/(((1)/(9)))|= − (1)/(3)]

  • Sequence III is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term: [MATH: (a_{2})/(a_{1}) = (8)/(4)|= 2; (a_{3})/(a_{2}) = (12)/(8)|= (3)/(2)]

In conclusion, only sequences I and II could be geometric sequences.

[MATH: 3|= (12)/(x); 3x|= 12; x|= 4.]

Which of the sequences below are geometric sequences?

1. [MATH: 2, \: 4, \: 8, \: 16, \: \ldots]
2. [MATH: 1, \: -\dfrac{1}{3}, \: \dfrac{1}{9}, \: -\dfrac{1}{27}, \: \ldots]
3. [MATH: 4, \: 8, \: 12, \: 16, \: \ldots]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A sequence is geometric if there is a common ratio between its terms. Let's check each sequence in turn.

- Sequence I is geometric. For each pair of consecutive terms, the common ratio is the same:
[MATH: (a_{2})/(a_{1}) = (4)/(2)|= 2; (a_{3})/(a_{2}) = (8)/(4)|= 2; (a_{4})/(a_{3}) = (16)/(8)|= 2]
- Sequence II is also geometric. Again, for each pair of consecutive terms, the common ratio is the same:
[MATH: (a_{2})/(a_{1}) = ((− (1)/(3)))/(1)|= − (1)/(3); (a_{3})/(a_{2}) = (((1)/(9)))/((− (1)/(3)))|= − (1)/(3); (a_{4})/(a_{3}) = ((− (1)/(27)))/(((1)/(9)))|= − (1)/(3)]
- Sequence III is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:
[MATH: (a_{2})/(a_{1}) = (8)/(4)|= 2; (a_{3})/(a_{2}) = (12)/(8)|= (3)/(2)]

In conclusion, only sequences I and II could be geometric sequences.
